items.prompt: Define business activity.
items.canonical_answer: Business activity is the process of combining resources - natural, human and man-made - to produce goods or services that satisfy the wants and needs of customers.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. No example and no evaluation required.

items.prompt: Explain why a business needs revenue from customers whatever purpose it was set up to serve.
items.canonical_answer: Because revenue is what pays for the resources the business uses. A privately owned firm pursuing profit, a state-owned utility pursuing a service objective and a social enterprise pursuing a social aim all have to buy materials, pay wages and maintain equipment. An organisation producing something customers do not want, or cannot afford at the price charged, tends to exhaust its money and stop trading; a subsidy can postpone that point but it does not remove the requirement to cover what the resources cost.
marking_guidance: Reason: revenue is what pays for the resources used, so the requirement holds whatever the stated purpose.
The answer must say why the purpose does not change the requirement, not only list purposes.

items.prompt: A municipal water utility is required to supply households in an outlying settlement where the pipeline costs more to maintain than the households pay for water. A bottled-water company in the same town refuses to deliver there. Explain what this shows about the purpose of business activity.
items.canonical_answer: It shows that the purpose depends on ownership. The utility is publicly owned and carries a service objective set by government, so it supplies the settlement even though that route does not cover its own cost, and the shortfall is met from revenue elsewhere or from public funds. The bottler is privately owned and pursues profit for its owners, so a route whose revenue is below its cost is one it declines. The two are not disagreeing about the facts - both know the route loses money - they are answering to different objectives.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the facts given - a route whose cost exceeds what households pay, and two differently owned businesses.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that ownership sets the objective, which is why the same figures lead to opposite decisions.
Conclusion: must reach a statement about the purpose of business activity, not merely describe both businesses.

items.prompt: Explain how a business that produces something customers do not value reaches the point of closing.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that customers value the output at less than the price asked, so they buy elsewhere or not at all. Revenue is what pays for the resources the business uses, so the mechanism is simple subtraction: wages, rent and materials continue at the rate the business set them, while the money coming in is below that rate. The owner covers the gap from savings or from credit, which works while either lasts. As the gap continues the business falls behind with suppliers, supply on credit stops, and it can no longer produce even for the customers it does have. The consequence is that it ceases trading, and the owners - who are paid after suppliers, employees and lenders - take the loss.
marking_guidance: Condition: the starting point is output customers value at less than the price asked.
Mechanism: costs continue while revenue falls short, because revenue is what pays for the resources.
Consequence: the reserves or credit covering the gap run out and supply stops.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the survival of the business and the loss falling on the owners.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to say that the purpose of every business is to make a profit?
items.canonical_answer: Because profit is the purpose of one kind of owner, not of business activity itself. Privately owned firms usually pursue profit for their owners. State-owned and public-sector organisations pursue a service objective set by government and may be required to serve areas a profit-seeking firm would leave. Social enterprises pursue a social or environmental aim while still needing to cover their costs. What they share is the need for revenue to pay for resources, which is not the same thing as a profit objective.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must say why the belief is wrong - the objective follows from ownership - and not only that it is.
Reward the distinction between needing revenue and having a profit objective.

items.prompt: Identify the four factors of production and what each one contributes to output.
items.canonical_answer: Land - the natural resources the business uses: its site and the water, minerals, timber, grazing and climate it draws on. Labour - the human effort, physical and mental, that people supply in producing goods and services. Capital - the man-made resources used in production: machinery, vehicles, buildings and equipment. Enterprise - the willingness and ability to bring the other three together, decide what to produce and how, and carry the risk that the venture makes a loss.
marking_guidance: All four must be identified and each given its own contribution.

items.prompt: A zinc refinery and a 200-seat call centre are built in the same industrial park. Explain how the factors of production they use differ, and why that matters to each business.
items.canonical_answer: The refinery is capital-intensive: most of what it uses is plant, furnaces and handling equipment, with a comparatively small workforce. The call centre is labour-intensive: its main resource is 200 people, with modest equipment behind each of them. This matters because it tells each business where its costs sit and what kind of change hurts it. A rise in wage rates lands on most of the call centre's cost base and on a small part of the refinery's. A rise in the cost of electricity or of imported machinery does the reverse. It also shapes how quickly each can cut costs if demand falls: the call centre can reduce shifts, while the refinery's plant has to be paid for whether it runs or not.

Reasoning: the mechanism is that the dominant factor determines where the cost base sits.

items.prompt: Explain how the absence of enterprise leaves land, labour and capital producing nothing.
items.canonical_answer: Because the other three factors are inputs and none of them decides anything. A plot, a group of unemployed workers and an idle vehicle each have a use, but nothing in them determines which use, in what order, for which customer, or at what price. Enterprise is the willingness and ability to bring them together, make those decisions, and carry the risk that the answer turns out to be wrong. Until somebody does that and accepts the consequences of being wrong, the three sit apart and output is zero. That is why enterprise is described as organising the other three rather than as a fourth item beside them.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must explain how the other three remain inert - they supply capacity but make no decision - rather than asserting that enterprise is important.

items.prompt: A leather workshop in Okahandja buys hides, thread and fittings costing N$260 for each bag it makes and sells the bag for N$690. It sold 180 bags last month. Calculate the added value per bag and the total added value for the month.
items.canonical_answer: Added value per unit = selling price per unit - cost of bought-in materials and components per unit. Substituting: N$690 - N$260 = N$430 per bag. Total added value = N$430 x 180 = N$77 400 for the month. Interpretation: N$77 400 is what the workshop has to cover its wages, rent, power, insurance and marketing from, and whatever is left after those is its profit for the month.

Interpretation: the answer must say what the figure means - the amount available to meet the workshop's own costs before profit - and not stop at the number.

items.prompt: A workshop making leather bags sells them wholesale at N$690 with a bought-in cost of N$260. It is considering stamping its own maker's mark on each bag and guaranteeing the stitching for five years. Explain how this would raise its added value and what it depends on.

What they can change is the price customers accept, so if buyers pay N$760 instead of N$690, added value per bag rises from N$430 to N$500. The whole of the increase depends on customers seeing a difference worth paying for - the guarantee has to be believed and the mark has to mean something to them. Where they do not see it, the higher price tends to cost sales volume, and total added value can fall even though added value per bag has risen.

items.prompt: Explain how raising the price of a product can raise added value per unit and reduce total added value at the same time.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that customers do not see a difference worth the higher price. The mechanism is that added value per unit is the price less the bought-in cost, so raising the price raises it arithmetically and immediately; but the quantity sold is set by customers, and a price rise they do not accept moves some of them to a competitor or out of the market. The consequence is that total added value, which is added value per unit multiplied by units sold, moves in whichever direction the larger of the two effects points. A workshop selling 180 bags at N$690 against a bought-in cost of N$260 generates N$430 x 180 = N$77 400. At N$760 the per-unit figure rises to N$500, but if volume falls to 120 bags total added value is N$500 x 120 = N$60 000 - a fall of N$17 400 in the month. The effect on the business is that its ability to cover wages and rent has weakened even though the per-unit figure it was watching improved.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain starts from customers not seeing a difference worth the higher price.
Mechanism: per-unit added value is arithmetic and immediate; volume is decided by customers.
Consequence: total added value is the product of the two, so it can fall while the per-unit figure rises, and the size of the fall must be calculated rather than asserted.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the money the business has available to cover its own costs.

items.prompt: A guesthouse owner spends every Friday doing the bookkeeping herself, which would cost N$2 600 a month to outsource. items.prompt: Explain how ignoring opportunity cost leads a business to make a decision that is worse than the one it could have made.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the business has more than one use for the same scarce resource and judges each use on its own. The mechanism is the test it applies: asking whether an option earns something rather than whether it earns more than the best alternative. Any option with a positive return passes that test, so the business commits the resource to the first acceptable use it finds. The consequence is that the resource earns less than it could have: if a vehicle returns N$150 000 and a refit would have returned N$210 000, choosing the vehicle costs the business N$60 000 a year it never sees. The effect on the business is a lower profit than was available, and because the shortfall never appears in the accounts - the vehicle shows a genuine N$150 000 - nothing in the records prompts anybody to look for it.

Mechanism: the wrong test - positive return rather than best available return - is what admits the weaker option.
Consequence: the resource earns less than it could, and the size of the shortfall must be stated.

items.prompt: A town council owns one serviced plot. It can grant it to a clinic, to a business park or to a sports ground, and there is demand for all three. Explain what this situation illustrates about economic activity.
items.canonical_answer: It illustrates scarcity, choice and opportunity cost together. The plot is a scarce resource: there is one of it and three wants for it, which is what scarcity means - not that the town is poor, but that the resource cannot satisfy every want placed on it. Because any use rules out the others, a choice cannot be avoided; declining to decide is itself a decision to leave the plot idle. And whichever use is granted, the opportunity cost is the benefit of the single next best of the remaining two, which is why the council has to rank them rather than simply show that its chosen use is worthwhile.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the council's own situation - one plot, three competing uses.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that a scarce resource used one way cannot be used another.
Conclusion: must reach all three ideas - scarcity, unavoidable choice, and the next best alternative as the cost.

items.prompt: The rand falls 15% against the US dollar. A Windhoek hair salon buying almost everything locally and an electronics dealer whose entire stock is imported from Asia both trade in the same street. Explain why the effect on them differs.
items.canonical_answer: Because the two businesses have very different exposure to the thing that changed. The Namibian dollar is pegged one-for-one with the rand, so a fall of the rand against the dollar raises the Namibian dollar price of goods bought from outside the Common Monetary Area. For the electronics dealer that is the whole stock, so the 15% lands on most of its cost base, and it either raises prices into a market that may not follow or absorbs the rise and watches its margin narrow. For the salon, imported appliances are a small part of one year's spending; its main costs are wages and rent, which are unaffected. The change is identical for both; the size of the effect is set by how much of each business's spending is exposed to it.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the two businesses given - one buying locally, one importing its whole stock.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the effect reaches a business through costs, scaled by its exposure.
Conclusion: must reach the difference in the size of the effect and what each business can do about it.

items.prompt: Explain how a change in the external environment works through to a fall in a business's profit.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the change touches something the business actually buys or sells. The mechanism is that every external change reaches a business through one of two doors: its revenue, if the change moves what customers will buy or what they will pay, or its costs, if it moves what the business pays for inputs, labour or borrowing. The consequence is scaled by exposure: the proportion of the business's sales or spending attached to the thing that changed. A 15% rise in the cost of an input that is 5% of spending costs less than one per cent of total cost; the same rise on an input that is 70% of spending takes more than ten per cent. Profit then falls by the amount the business cannot pass on to customers or absorb by cutting elsewhere. The effect on the business is that a firm which monitors the change and adjusts what it offers - resourcing locally, repricing, fixing a contract - tends to keep more of its customers and its margin than one that does not.
marking_guidance: Condition: the change must touch something the business buys or sells.
Mechanism: the change enters through revenue or through costs, and exposure scales it.
Consequence: the fall in profit is what cannot be passed on or absorbed, and the size must be tied to the proportion of spending exposed.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and the difference monitoring makes.

items.prompt: Explain why a business can be profitable and still fail.
items.canonical_answer: Because profit and cash are recorded at different moments. Profit is recorded when a sale is made; cash arrives when the customer pays. A business selling on credit records the profit in the month of the sale but receives the money thirty or sixty days later, while wages are paid weekly and suppliers expect payment on their own terms. If the money going out runs ahead of the money coming in for long enough, the business cannot pay what it owes when it is owed. Suppliers then withhold further supply, it cannot produce, and it stops trading - having recorded a profit in every month of the process.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must explain why the two figures differ in timing, not merely assert that they are different.

items.prompt: A construction firm in Swakopmund completes a N$900 000 government contract in March and is paid in late May. Explain how a firm in this position can fail despite the contract being profitable.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is a gap between paying for the work and being paid for it: the firm pays wages every Friday through February and March and settles its builders' merchant at thirty days, while the N$900 000 arrives in late May. The mechanism is that the bank balance carries that gap. With the profit recorded in March but no cash until May, the balance falls below what the March and April wage bills need. The consequence follows in order: the merchant is paid late and puts the account on hold; without materials the next contract cannot start; with no next contract there is no further revenue to close the gap, and the May receipt arrives at a firm that has already stopped working. The effect on the business is failure through illiquidity, and the stakeholders who feel it first are the employees waiting on wages and the merchant waiting on the account.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain starts from the gap between paying for the work and being paid for it.
Mechanism: profit recorded in March does not put cash in the bank until May.
Consequence: late payment to the merchant stops supply, which stops the next contract.

The same event is therefore a setback for one and a threat to survival for the other.

items.prompt: Explain how expanding faster than it can finance causes a growing business to fail.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is that growth consumes cash before it produces it. Winning more orders means buying more materials, taking on more staff and often larger premises, and all of that is paid for in advance of the sales it supports. The sales are then made on credit, so the money returns thirty or sixty days after the costs went out. Each additional order therefore widens the gap between money leaving and money arriving, and the faster the business grows the wider the gap gets. Because the business is profitable and its order book is full, nothing in the trading figures looks wrong, which is why the problem is usually noticed only when a payment cannot be met. At that point suppliers withhold credit, the business cannot fulfil the orders it has won, and it fails while growing.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must explain how each additional order widens the gap between money going out and money coming in, not simply assert that growth is risky.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume that an injection of finance will save a failing business?
items.canonical_answer: Because failure usually has several causes acting together rather than one. Where the underlying problem is a market that is smaller than the owners thought, costs that are not controlled, or management without the relevant experience, the finance is spent at the same rate as before and the business arrives at the same position a few months later, now owing more. The same applies to a price cut, which raises volume and lowers the margin on every unit. A single remedy fixes a business whose problem was single.

items.prompt: Identify, in order, the stages an entrepreneur goes through in turning an idea into a trading business, and what each stage produces.
items.canonical_answer: Begin by identifying the opportunity: the unmet want and the customers who have it. Then research the market, starting from what can be observed - how many such customers there are, what they pay now and who already serves them - which produces the evidence the rest depends on. Next write the business plan, which turns that research into forecasts of sales, costs and cash and produces the figure for how much finance is needed. Then raise that finance, from own savings, family, a bank, a development fund or an investor. Then choose and register a legal form - sole trader, partnership or company - with the licences and tax registrations that go with it, which produces the legal entity that can contract. Skipping the research and the plan does not remove them; it moves the discovery of a flaw from week three to month eight, after the equipment has been bought.

items.prompt: A government is deciding how to encourage more people to start businesses and is considering putting all of its budget into a start-up finance scheme. Evaluate whether that is the most effective use of the money.

The decisive criterion is that the barriers differ from one would-be entrepreneur to the next, so a single instrument reaches only the people whose obstacle it matches. A finance scheme helps the person with a researched idea, the skills to run it and no money. It does nothing for the person with money and no tested idea, and for that person it does harm, because cheap finance makes it easier to commit to a venture nobody has checked. In the context of a country where lack of business skills, the time and cost of registration and unreliable infrastructure are documented obstacles alongside finance, a budget split across finance, training and mentoring, and simplified registration reaches more of the population of would-be founders per dollar spent.

There is also an administrative case - one scheme is cheaper to run than four.

On balance the money should be split, with finance as the largest single share but not the whole. The judgement would change if evidence showed that in this country the other barriers were already being addressed by other bodies, or if the schemes were so small that splitting them left each one below the size at which it does anything.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between risk and uncertainty in business.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is whether a likelihood can be attached. Risk is a possible outcome whose likelihood can be estimated from experience or data, so it can be planned for, insured against or reduced: a bakery whose records show that about 6% of loaves go unsold each day faces a risk it can price into its costing. Uncertainty is a possible future event whose likelihood cannot meaningfully be estimated, because there is no comparable experience to judge it from: the chance that a new disease closes the border next year is an uncertainty, and no percentage can honestly be put on it. The consequence is that the two are handled by different tools - calculation for one, reserves and flexibility for the other.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: the difference is whether a likelihood can be estimated, and the consequence for how each is handled must be stated.

A border closure is an uncertainty: there is no comparable record to put a percentage on, so no premium can be calculated for it and no deposit policy covers it. It is handled differently in kind - cash reserves large enough to survive a season at half capacity, short vehicle-hire agreements rather than long ones, and a domestic market developed so that no single source country carries the business.

items.prompt: Explain how selling into several different markets reduces a business's exposure to risk.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is that the events which move demand in one market are largely different from those which move it in another. A tour operator whose customers all come from one country loses a third of its bookings if that country's airline reroutes, its currency falls, or its households cut spending; the same operator drawing a third of its trade from domestic customers, a third from Germany and a third from South Africa loses only the affected share, and the other two continue. Spreading does not make any one of those events less likely. What it changes is how much of the business each event can reach, so the range within which total revenue moves narrows even though the range for each market does not. The limit is that it works only for events specific to a market: a global downturn moves all three together, and against that kind of event spreading offers little protection.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must explain how independent sources of demand narrow the range of total revenue, and must state the limit - shared shocks move all markets together.

items.prompt: Explain why processing a raw material at home raises a country's income more than exporting it unprocessed.
items.canonical_answer: Because the country keeps the value added in the processing as well as the price of the raw material. Exporting raw hides earns the price of hides and nothing else; the tanning, the cutting and the finishing are done abroad, so the value those stages add accrues to businesses and workers in another country. Tanning the hides at home and exporting finished leather earns the price of the leather, which is the price of the hides plus the value the tannery adds - and the wages of the people who add it are paid and spent locally, and the tannery's profits are taxed locally. The raw material is the same; what changes is how many stages of value are captured before it leaves.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that encouraging new small businesses is the most effective way for a developing country to raise incomes.
items.canonical_answer:
It is effective but not sufficient on its own, and the judgement should be that small-business encouragement works best as one part of a wider policy. The decisive criterion is survival. New businesses create jobs and incomes, widen the tax base and use local resources, and the incomes they pay circulate locally so that the effect is multiplied. But those effects accrue only while the businesses trade, and new businesses fail more often than established ones - so a policy measured by the number started rather than the number still trading after three years can look successful while raising incomes very little. The conditions that make the difference are the same ones the development argument rests on: whether the businesses grow, whether they employ and train local people, and whether profits are reinvested in the country.

The strongest argument against relying on small businesses is that raising incomes substantially requires productivity, and very small enterprises in crowded local markets - another kiosk selling what four kiosks already sell - tend to divide existing demand rather than add output. On that view investment in skills, infrastructure and larger enterprises does more per dollar.

The balanced position is that encouraging small business raises incomes where it is paired with the things that let those businesses survive and grow: training, reliable power and transport, and access to markets beyond the immediate town. The judgement would change if the local market were already well supplied, in which case the same money spent on skills or on export access would do more.

Context: the answer must be argued for a developing country, using the conditions that determine the development effect.
Criterion: the decisive factor is survival and growth, not the number of businesses started.
Counterargument: must address the case that very small enterprises divide existing demand rather than adding output.

items.prompt: Explain how the financial forecasts section of a business plan is built up, stage by stage.
items.canonical_answer: Begin with start-up costs: the premises deposit, equipment, initial stock, registration and licence fees - everything that must be paid before the business can open. Take as inputs the figures the earlier sections produced: the sales volume and price from the market research, and the costs of premises, equipment, suppliers and staff from the operations plan. Next calculate forecast revenue, which is price multiplied by the forecast volume for each period, and set beside it the forecast costs for the same periods, separating those that change with output from those that do not. Then build the cash-flow forecast month by month, entering each receipt and each payment in the month it actually moves rather than the month the sale is made. Then carry out the break-even calculation, which states the output at which revenue covers total cost. Finish with what the section produces: the amount of finance required, which is the largest cumulative cash shortfall the monthly forecast reveals, plus a margin.

The judgement is therefore to answer those three questions in writing, on a page, and keep it current, rather than to produce a document she will not revisit and that will date as soon as a second stall opens. What the plan is still good for is its record of the assumptions behind the 900 - which customers, at what price, how often - because comparing those assumptions with what has actually happened shows whether the shortfall is the new competitor, the price, or a market that was always smaller. The figure should then be replaced with a forecast made for the market that now exists.

items.prompt: Explain how a plan written to impress a provider of finance can end up damaging the business it was written for.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the plan's purpose was to obtain money rather than to guide the venture, so its figures were chosen for how they read. The mechanism is that the same document is then used for a second job it was not built for. Once trading begins the forecasts become the benchmark the owner compares actual performance against, because they are the only forecasts that exist. The consequence is a persistent, misleading variance: actual sales fall short of a number that was never a serious estimate, month after month. The owner responds to a problem that is partly an artefact of the document - cutting prices, cutting marketing, or abandoning a product that was performing acceptably against any honest forecast. The effect on the business is decisions taken against a false standard, and on the relationship with the provider of finance, a record of missed forecasts that makes the next request harder.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain starts from a plan whose figures were chosen to persuade rather than to forecast.
Mechanism: the same forecasts are reused as the benchmark for monitoring, because no others exist.
Consequence: a persistent variance that is an artefact of the document prompts corrective action that was not needed.

items.prompt: Kalahari Preserves buys fruit and jars costing N$26 for each jar of jam it makes and sells the jar for N$58. It sold 4 200 jars last month. The owner can spend N$180 000 either on a labelling machine that she expects would let her charge N$66 a jar at the same volume, or on a second cooking vessel that she expects would raise volume to 6 000 jars a month at the present price. Calculate the current added value per jar and for the month, calculate the monthly added value under each option, and evaluate which option she should choose.
items.canonical_answer:
Now: added value per jar = N$58 - N$26 = N$32. Monthly added value = N$32 x 4 200 = N$134 400.

Labelling machine: added value per jar = N$66 - N$26 = N$40, and at 4 200 jars monthly added value = N$40 x 4 200 = N$168 000, an increase of N$33 600 a month.

Second vessel: added value per jar stays at N$32, and at 6 000 jars monthly added value = N$32 x 6 000 = N$192 000, an increase of N$57 600 a month.

Judgement: she should buy the second vessel. The decisive criterion is which increase is less dependent on an assumption she cannot test. The vessel's N$57 600 requires that the extra 1 800 jars sell at the price she already achieves, which her present trade is evidence for. The machine's N$33 600 requires customers to accept a 14% price rise, and if even part of the volume is lost the gain narrows sharply: at N$40 of added value a jar she needs 4 200 jars to reach N$168 000, and at 3 500 jars the machine yields N$40 x 3 500 = N$140 000, barely above the present N$134 400. Choosing either has an opportunity cost of the other, and on these figures the forgone option is worth N$33 600 a month if she takes the vessel and N$57 600 if she takes the machine.

The strongest argument for the machine is that better labelling may be what lets her reach retailers she cannot supply now, in which case it raises volume as well as price - but that is a different case from the one costed, and it needs a retailer's commitment to support it. The condition on the recommendation is that the extra 1 800 jars can actually be sold: if her present volume is limited by demand rather than by cooking capacity, the second vessel adds capacity she cannot use and the machine becomes the better choice.
marking_guidance: All the stated figures must be calculated with working shown.
Judgement: the answer must recommend one option, not present both and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Kalahari Preserves' own figures and on what its present trade is evidence for.
Criterion: the decisive factor is which gain depends least on an untested assumption.
Counterargument: must address the case for the labelling machine, including the possibility that it raises volume as well as price.
Condition: must state what would reverse the recommendation - whether output is limited by demand or by capacity.

items.prompt: Hilma has N$60 000 of savings and a signed order from one guest lodge for laundry services worth N$18 000 a month. A machine large enough for the lodge costs N$95 000; she has been offered N$40 000 of external finance secured against her vehicle, leaving a gap. The lodge's contract runs for twelve months and it takes 70% of her forecast revenue. Analyse the barriers she faces and the risks she is taking on, and evaluate whether she should proceed.
items.canonical_answer:
Barriers first. The binding one is finance: N$60 000 of her own plus N$40 000 offered is N$100 000 against a machine at N$95 000, which leaves N$5 000 for installation, detergent, transport and the first month's working capital. That is a half-financed position of the kind that buys the equipment and runs out before the business is trading properly. The finance is offered on security rather than on trade, which is what happens where there is no trading record, and it puts her vehicle at stake. The second barrier is the opportunity cost of whatever she gives up to run this, and the third is scale - she cannot yet reach the cost per kilogram a larger competitor can.

Risks and uncertainties differ here and should be separated. Machine breakdown is a risk: it has a knowable failure rate, it can be reduced by a service agreement and transferred in part by insurance. Late payment by the lodge is a risk she can estimate once she has a few months of history, and can reduce by agreeing terms in writing. Dependence on one customer for 70% of revenue is closer to an uncertainty: whether that lodge renews in twelve months turns on its own occupancy, its owners' decisions and tourist arrivals, none of which she has a record to put a percentage on. What answers an uncertainty is not a calculation but flexibility and reserves - a second customer, and cash held back.

Recommendation: she should proceed, but not on these numbers. The decisive factor is the N$5 000 remaining after the machine, which leaves no capacity to absorb a single late payment or an early breakdown - the ordinary events she can predict, not the extraordinary ones. She should either negotiate a smaller or second-hand machine that leaves N$20 000 to N$25 000 of working capital, or secure a second customer before committing, which reduces the 70% dependence at the same time.

The strongest argument against waiting is that the signed order is worth N$18 000 a month now and may go elsewhere, and that no start-up ever has enough working capital. That is fair, and it is why the recommendation is to proceed rather than to abandon it. The condition is the working-capital margin: if she can reduce the equipment cost or obtain a second contract, she should start; if she cannot do either, committing her vehicle to a venture with N$5 000 of headroom and one customer is a risk out of proportion to the N$18 000 a month it is being taken for.
marking_guidance: Both the barriers and the exposures must be analysed before the recommendation is reached.
Judgement: a recommendation is required.
Context: the answer must use Hilma's own figures - the N$60 000, the N$40 000 offer, the N$95 000 machine and the 70% dependence.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the working capital left after the equipment is bought.
Counterargument: must address the case for proceeding now, given a signed order that may not wait.
Condition: must state what would change the recommendation.
Risk and uncertainty must be separated on whether a likelihood can be estimated, not merely listed together.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: A family engineering workshop with fourteen employees, trading profitably for nine years, is considering opening a second branch in another town at a cost of N$1.4 million, of which N$900 000 would be borrowed. The owners have never written a business plan. Evaluate whether they should write one before deciding.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: yes, and mainly for themselves rather than for the bank.

Paragraph 1 - what makes this different from the last nine years. The workshop's success so far is evidence about one town and one set of customers. The second branch is a new market, and none of the knowledge that has carried the business is evidence about it.

Paragraph 2 - the external purpose. N$900 000 is being borrowed, and a provider of finance decides on evidence that the money will come back. A plan with researched demand in the new town, costed operations and a month-by-month cash-flow forecast gives them that evidence; its absence usually means less offered, a higher price, or more security demanded. Nine years of accounts help, but they describe the existing branch.

Paragraph 3 - the internal purpose, which is the stronger one here. The research the plan forces - who the customers in the new town are, what they pay, who serves them now - is the only thing that can test the assumption that what works in one town works in another. The cash-flow forecast also answers a question the profit forecast does not: how far the existing branch's cash has to stretch while the new one establishes itself.

Paragraph 4 - the limitations, taken seriously. The forecasts will rest on assumptions and may be wrong; the plan will date; it takes weeks the owners could spend on the existing trade. And a plan written to satisfy the bank tends to carry optimistic figures that then make a poor benchmark for managing the branch.

Judgement and condition: they should write one, because the decisive factor is the size of the commitment relative to the business - N$1.4 million against a fourteen-person workshop, with N$900 000 of it borrowed against assets they already hold. The counterargument that nine profitable years are better evidence than any forecast is answered by pointing out that those years are evidence about a different market. It would be a different judgement for a N$60 000 expansion in the same town, where the existing trade genuinely is the evidence and the cost of being wrong is small.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay - structure with a stated judgement is what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must use the workshop's own facts - fourteen employees, nine profitable years, N$1.4 million with N$900 000 borrowed, a new town.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the size of the commitment relative to the business and the fact that the new market is untested.
Counterargument: must include the real case against - nine years of trading evidence, and the limitations of forecasts.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer, so the recommendation depends on stated circumstances.

items.prompt: A development agency is reviewing why so many of the businesses it funded three years ago have closed. Identify the questions it should ask about each closed business, and explain what the answer to each would tell it.
items.canonical_answer:
Did it run out of cash, and was it profitable when it did? State this one first because the two answers point in opposite directions. A profitable business that ran out of cash had a timing problem - money going out before customers paid - and the remedy is working capital or better terms. A business that was not profitable had a trading problem, and more cash would have postponed the closure rather than prevented it.

Was there a market at the price assumed? The answer separates a business that could not sell from one that could not sell profitably. Each of these agency-funded businesses had a forecast; comparing it with what was actually sold shows whether the research behind it was done.

Had the owner run a business before, or worked in that trade? Inexperience shows up in specific ways - pricing below cost, no records, stock ordered late - and the answer tells the agency whether training alongside the finance would have changed the outcome.

Did costs move away from the plan, and which ones? This separates a cost the owner could control from one imposed from outside, such as a supplier's price or a regulation.

Was it growing when it closed? A business that failed while expanding was consuming cash faster than it generated it, which is a different failure from a shrinking one and needs a different remedy.

What else was happening at the same time? Failure usually has several causes acting together, so the agency should expect two or three of these answers to be yes for each business - and should be suspicious of a review that finds a single cause, because the single-cause explanation is what makes a single remedy look sufficient.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what a particular answer would tell the agency.
Context: these are questions about businesses the agency itself funded, so each answer must be tied to what the agency could have done differently.
The review must end on the point that failure usually has several causes, and that a single-cause finding should be treated with suspicion.

items.prompt: Namib Hides tans leather at one plant in Okahandja and exports 80% of its output to Italy, invoicing in euro. Its costs are almost all in Namibian dollars. It is considering buying a small finishing plant near Milan so that it can supply Italian customers from inside Italy. Analyse how this would change the business and evaluate whether it should proceed.
items.canonical_answer:
What it is now and what it would become. Namib Hides is an international business: it sells to customers in another country but all its production is in Namibia. Buying the Milan plant would make it multinational, because it would then control production operations in more than one country. Nothing about its customers needs to change for that; the test is where it produces.

What changes with it. Four things move together. Finance: a plant is paid for before it earns, and for a single-site tannery that is a large commitment. Management: a site the owners can visit a few times a year has to run without them, so the business needs managers it does not currently employ. Compliance: a second legal and tax system, with Italian employment rules, standards and returns. And currency exposure changes shape rather than size. At present 80% of revenue is in euro against costs almost entirely in Namibian dollars, so a fall in the euro cuts the local-currency value of nearly all its sales with no offsetting fall in costs. With Italian wages and inputs paid in euro, part of the cost base would move with the revenue, which narrows that exposure - this is the one respect in which the move reduces risk rather than adding to it.

Recommendation: it should not proceed yet. The decisive factor is that the problem it is solving - currency exposure and proximity to customers - can be addressed with less commitment. Forward cover or invoicing part of its sales in Namibian dollars addresses the exposure without buying a plant, and a finishing arrangement with an existing Italian processor tests whether local finishing wins the orders it hopes for before N$-millions and a management structure are committed.

The strongest argument for proceeding is that customers who want short lead times may be unreachable from Okahandja at any price, in which case the plant is not an efficiency measure but the only route to that segment, and the delay costs orders. The condition is therefore evidence from the customers themselves: if Italian buyers state that they will place work with a local finisher and not with an importer, the case changes and the plant becomes worth the management load. Without that evidence, a single-site business is taking on a second country to solve a problem that has cheaper solutions.
marking_guidance: The change of category and the changes that follow from it must both be analysed before the recommendation.
Judgement: a recommendation is required.
Context: the answer must use Namib Hides' own facts - one plant, 80% euro revenue, costs in Namibian dollars.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether the same problem can be solved with a smaller commitment.
Counterargument: must address the case that some customers are unreachable from a single Namibian site.
Condition: must state the evidence that would reverse the recommendation.
